item.title: The Physics of Beer Foam
item.dc:creator: Dylan Standen
item.description:
Who doesn’t love a good (ice-cold) beer? I certainly do, and if you have ever wondered if there is a mathematical way to describe the foam from pouring a beer, then you have come to right place. In this post I am going to explore and explain the Physics that make this effect occur and how we can describe it mathematically. Towards the end I will discuss the surprisingly deep overlap with integrable systems - systems which are exactly solvable, by which we mean we can integrate them to attain a solution.

The Advent of Beer

Beer is one of the oldest alcoholic beverages. It’s root stretch back to at least 13,000, with the Natufians consuming a beer-like beverage during ritual ceremonies. Obviously since then, peoples across the world have been fermenting grain and hops in order to create the beautiful golden drink we know today.

Enough about the history of beer and onto maths. I should note that I will not be covering the chemistry/physics of how the foam actually forms, I will instead be focussing on the mathematical laws that govern its behavior.

Foam Drainage Equation

The dynamics of how Foam evolves, known as the foam drainage equation (or law) was first formalised in 1996 with the work by Verbist, Weaire & Kraynik.

item.title: Curvature, Curvature, Curvature!
item.dc:creator: Dylan Standen
item.description:
Introduction

What is curvature? Well, it’s a good question and one that can’t be answered naively. Developing the notion of curvature (along with a formal mathematical definition) took years as well as some of the greatest mathematical minds to finally crack. Given this, I think it would be useful to discuss the history and development of this topic first before turning to physics.

All Roads Lead to Euler

As with most things in mathematics their origins lead to Leonhard Euler. I should mention that while curvature as a concept dates back to the time of the ancient Greeks, it was only later, after the advent of Calculus, that we could formulate an analytical understanding of curvature.

So, Euler was interested in the curvature of curves and surfaces. This led him to define quantities called principal curvatures. The theorem that led to this concept was first proved by Euler in 1760.

The Curvature of Curves

You hopefully have an understanding of curves. The most famous example of one is simply a circle in . We can view this as the set of tuples such that

where I have set the radius equal to 1 for ease. This view isn’t as useful for our needs, however. Instead, I will introduce a polar coordinate transformation such that

A circle can then be viewed as a closed curve parametrised by a single variable . This curve view extends nicely to 3D (the first space where differential geometry was studied). Let’s introduce a curve , which is parametrised by a parameter , i.e. 

If I have such a curve, how do I measure its length? For that we need the arc length formula.

Let a point on the curve be given by position vector , which is centered at the origin. Suppose, I look at a new position on the curve an infinitesimal distance away from , given by . The separation vector is given (to first order using Taylors theorem)

This little (actually infinitesimal) separation vector has some length given by everyone’s favourite Theorem; the Pythagorean theorem,

The arc length of a certain section of this curve is then simply the sum (actually the integral) of all of these infinitesimal distances

Where the natural measure is the parameter . I’ll now make a slight change of notation to make the expression more general. Let (the indexing set) and take . With this we have

I should mention that the terms inside the square root are the squares of the velocity components in each direction. The above can be written in an even more succinct way by introducing the metric.

The Metric

The metric allows us to define distances and angles on our surface, think of it as a map

where is a vector space (if you don’t recall the definition that’s fine just think of it as a space in which vectors live and obey certain axioms). So, we can see that it takes in two vectors and produces a real number. For the geometry we are considering here, this map is linear in both vectors, symmetric, and positive-definite. The last condition simply means that for any non-zero vector , allowing us to interpret as its length. How can we define such a map using vectors, well the logical choice is the inner product. The metric gives a more general form of it, however. Suppose that we have some basis for (where ) such that any element is

Similarly, let be another vector with components . Since the metric is linear in both of its arguments, we can write

We now define the components of the metric in this basis as

and hence

Writing out all of these sums quickly becomes quite tedious. Einstein introduced a convention where any index that appears twice in a term, once upstairs and once downstairs, is automatically summed over. This is called the Einstein summation convention. Using it, we can simply write

The sums have not disappeared; we have just agreed not to write them in order to save our sanity. In the usual Cartesian basis of , the components of the metric are , where is equal to 1 when and 0 otherwise (the identity matrix). Our infinitesimal distance can therefore be written as

For Cartesian coordinates this is just the Pythagorean theorem from before, hidden inside a much nicer piece of notation. Along our curve, each coordinate is a function of , so

Substituting this into the line element gives the arc length in its metric form,

In Euclidean space and this reduces to our previous expression. Notice also that it yields exactly the inner product we are used to. The usefulness of the metric is that we are no longer restricted to Cartesian coordinates, or even to flat spaces. In general the components may vary from point to point, in which case they should really be written as along the curve.

Parameterisation Invariance

The length of the curve is a physically meaningful object that we could measure in the lab. The arc length formula then should not depend on the parameter I use to “measure’’ the curve. We say it is parameterisation invariant. To see this, suppose I define a new parameter for my path . I will assume this map is smooth and monotonic, with (a requirement of the inverse function theorem), so that all I am doing is relabelling the points along the same curve. With this map, the derivatives vary by the chain rule,

For simplicity, take the reparameterisation to preserve orientation, meaning . Substituting the above into the arc length gives

This is exactly the same arc length formula that we started with (we could make a trivial change of variables), only written using instead of . The parameter has changed, along with the coordinate velocity of the curve, but its length has not. If the reparameterisation reverses orientation then an absolute value appears when taking the square root; the conclusion is still the same. Note that we could have also derived this using the Jacobian, which would be

such that the integral is

which yields exactly as before.

This simple example points towards a much more powerful idea. A reparameterisation is a diffeomorphism of the interval used to label the curve: a smooth and invertible map whose inverse is also smooth. We can generalise this from a one-dimensional interval to an entire smooth manifold. The coordinates we attach to points may change, but geometric quantities do not depend on those labels. This idea sits at the heart of the diffeomorphism invariance of general relativity.

Gauge invariance follows the same general philosophy, although it acts on internal degrees of freedom rather than on the coordinates of spacetime. Different choices of gauge can give different mathematical descriptions of the same physical configuration. This freedom is incredibly powerful: it allows us to choose whichever coordinates, parameters, or gauges make a problem easiest without changing the underlying physics. We will see later that curvature is one of the objects that survives these changes and captures the actual geometry or physical field.

Back to Curvature

With that discussion of the arc length over we can start discussing the actual curvature of the curves themselves. We introduce a curve as before and choose the parameter now to be the arc length itself. This is a viable choice since, for a regular curve, the speed is non-zero and the arc length is strictly increasing. The inverse function theorem then allows us to invert and write the curve as .

Before doing this, it is useful to see what our choice of parameter does to the velocity vector. For an arbitrary parameter , the velocity of the curve is

I am using velocity here in a geometric sense. It is only a physical velocity if is time. The length of this vector is the speed at which the curve is being traced out,

The above follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus. When we use arc length as the parameter, the velocity vector becomes

Thus, choosing the arc length simply normalises the velocity vector. We call the unit tangent vector, since

We are now finally in a position to define curvature. The tangent vector of a straight line never changes, while the tangent vector of a curved line does. It is therefore natural to define the curvature vector as the rate of change of the unit tangent vector with respect to arc length,

The curvature vector cannot point along the curve itself. To see this, we differentiate the fact that the tangent vector has unit length,

Therefore is perpendicular to and points in the direction in which the curve is turning. Finally, we define the curvature to be the length of the curvature vector,

A straight line has , while a curve whose tangent changes rapidly has a larger curvature. Whenever , we can define the unit normal vector , giving

This definition is enough for curves in . When the ambient space itself is curved, the ordinary derivative will need to be replaced by a covariant derivative. We will come back to this later.

The above definition should hopefully make intuitive sense. In the 1D case, our curve is simply a line in the real plane (like the functions you know and love). The velocity of this curve is then simply the rate of change of the function and the curvature is then the rate of change of this rate of change.

Euler’s Theorem on Normal Curvature

Let be a smooth, regular surface embedded in , and let . We choose a local unit normal vector field near . There is not just one normal plane at : every unit tangent vector determines one. It is the plane

which passes through and contains both and the normal to the surface. Near , the intersection of with is a plane curve whose tangent at is . We call this curve a normal section of the surface.

Suppose that is parametrised by arc length, with and . Its curvature vector at lies along the surface normal, so we define the signed normal curvature in the direction by

The sign depends on our choice of , but the magnitude does not. As we vary over all unit tangent vectors at , the normal curvature has a maximum and a minimum. These two extremal values, and , are the principal curvatures, and the directions in which they occur are the principal directions. When , the two principal directions are perpendicular.

Euler’s theorem tells us the normal curvature in every other direction. Let and be unit principal directions associated with and . Any unit tangent vector can then be written as

where is the angle between and . Euler’s theorem states that

We can derive this equation without introducing any new machinery. First, recall that the curvature vector of a unit-speed curve is perpendicular to its tangent vector . Since the curve lies on the surface, is also perpendicular to the surface normal . We can therefore define the vector

The three vectors form an orthonormal basis of . Because the curvature vector has no component along , it can be expanded as

where is called the geodesic curvature and is the normal curvature. We will return to the meaning of geodesic curvature later. For now, taking the inner product with gives

To determine how this quantity depends on the direction of the curve, choose a local parametrisation of the surface around . We choose the coordinates so that, at ,

Its tangent vector at is

Principal Curvature and the Second Fundamental Form

Gauss had a large impact on the classical study of differential geometry. He and Riemann are to thank for many of our modern concepts and notations. It’s only right then that I introduce the same ideas as above, but now in terms of objects called fundamental forms.

The First Fundamental Form

Let us look at a parametric surface within . We will first consider a surface that can be written as the graph of some function . Let’s choose two coordinates and such that the surface is described by a map given by

Here is playing the role of the -coordinate. Not every surface can be written globally in this way, but locally this is possible around any point where the surface does not fold vertically over the -plane. This is more than enough for what we want to do.

We now ask what happens when we move a small distance in either of our coordinates. Differentiating gives the two vectors

These vectors point along the two coordinate curves on the surface. It should be clear that they are linearly independent and therefore form a basis of the tangent plane. An infinitesimal displacement along the surface is then

Just as we did earlier for a curve, we can find the length of this displacement by taking its inner product with itself,

It is conventional to give these three inner products their own names,

For our graph surface they are

where I have used and similarly for . We can now write the squared distance as

This expression is called the first fundamental form, and it is usually denoted by . Now, the name sounds rather grand, but it is simply the metric induced on the surface by the ordinary Euclidean inner product in . In matrix notation we have

so this is exactly the same metric that we introduced earlier, only now written in the coordinates of the surface. Technically speaking this would be the pull-back of the Euclidean metric onto the surface, but I won’t be careful about this here.

To see what information it contains, let and be two vectors in the tangent plane,

The first fundamental form acts on these vectors as

Taking gives the length of a tangent vector, while taking two different vectors allows us to calculate the angle between them. The first fundamental form also gives us the length of any curve on the surface. If

We can even find areas. The vectors and span an infinitesimal parallelogram on the surface, so

Although , , and will change if we choose different coordinates, the lengths, angles, and areas calculated from them will not. This is why the first fundamental form describes the intrinsic geometry of the surface. It tells us what someone confined to the surface could measure without ever needing to look at the surrounding space.

This also fills in a small detail from our earlier derivation of Euler’s formula. There we chose coordinates aligned with the orthonormal principal directions and . At the point , this choice means

Consequently, the unit vector has coordinate components and , exactly as we used above. The first fundamental form controls these intrinsic measurements, but it does not yet tell us how the surface bends inside . For that we need the second fundamental form.

The Second Fundamental Form

I’ll now discuss the second fundamental form and its relation to the principal curvatures. Suppose that, similar to the above, the surface in question is given by an at least twice differentiable function . We translate and rotate our coordinates so that the point we care about is the origin and its tangent plane is the -plane. In other words,

The first derivatives vanish at the origin because the tangent plane is horizontal there. Expanding around this point using Taylor’s theorem gives

where all the derivatives on the right-hand side are evaluated at . Notice that the constant and linear terms have disappeared because of our choice of coordinates. The first non-trivial information about how the surface leaves its tangent plane is therefore contained in its second derivatives.

Let us now look along a unit direction in the tangent plane,

where, for the moment, and simply point along the - and -axes. The normal plane determined by intersects the graph in the curve

At this curve has unit tangent , while its second derivative points along the surface normal . Its signed curvature is consequently

This expression is a quadratic form on the tangent plane. It is the simplest version of the second fundamental form. For our graph, at the point where the tangent plane is horizontal, we can write

Admittedly, this looks suspiciously similar to the first fundamental form, but the two forms contain different information. The first uses inner products of the first derivatives of and measures lengths within the surface. The second uses the normal components of the second derivatives of and measures how the surface bends away from its tangent plane.

To make this definition work for a general parametrised surface , first define its unit normal vector by

We then introduce the coefficients

The second fundamental form is

Suppose that a tangent vector is written as

The two fundamental forms evaluated on this vector are

The first expression gives the squared length of , while the second gives the normal component of the curvature in that direction. The normal curvature is

Hopefully it is obvious that for a unit vector the denominator is simply one. This formula is useful because it separates the two pieces of geometry: tells us what counts as a unit direction, while tells us how much the surface bends in that direction.

The principal curvatures are the maximum and minimum values of this ratio. Equivalently, they are the two values of that solve

If we choose an orthonormal basis consisting of the principal directions (which are themselves the eigenvectors of this eigenvalue problem), the two forms take the particularly simple form

The mixed term has vanished, and a unit direction has components . Evaluating on this direction immediately gives

Gaussian Curvature

As the name of this section suggests this measure of curvature was introduced by Gauss. More specifically, it was introduced by him in his Theorema egregium; apparently meaning “Remarkable Theorem”. Sadly I don’t speak Latin, so a google translate had to suffice.

The Gaussian curvature as define by gauss is

The Shape Operator

and let us denote the the tangent vector to at by , i.e. 

At each point on our curve, the surface will have some normal vector . We can then compare this normal at any point along the curve with the normal at the origin of our curve by smoothly moving the normal back to the origin and then taking the change in the vectors to be

Where is what is called the ambient Parallel Transport Operator. You can likely notice the similarity between this and the derivative operator acting on a function. This is actually no coindience, but to speak about this explicitly I’ll have to introduce parallel transport.

Okay, so parallel transport sounds interesting. It is. I’ll firstly have to define the covariant derivative and how it acts on vector fields also. This is all starting to feel like a rabbit hole isn’t it. This is, however, necessary to really understand curvature from its foundations to how we use it in modern physics. By the end you’ll hopefully come around to this level depth. If not, then too bad.

Given a surface (lets say in once again) described as the graph of some function , the directional derivative tells us how much the height function changes in a certain direction. But what if we want to generalise to vector valued functions (also called vector fields), well this is where the covariant derivative comes in to play. In comparing vectors at different points on the manifold we could naively decide to just take the difference of the two vectors we want to compare, this however doesn’t work. This is because vectors at different points on our surface lie in different spaces, called tangent spaces. Think of this space as the space of all tangent vectors to our surface at a specific point. There is no canonical way for these two spaces to interact, so we need a way of brining one vector back so that they lie in the same tangent space without changing the vector at all.

Parallel Transport

Consider a smooth curve on our surface and a vector field along it, so that at each point the vector lies in the tangent space (which is commonly denoted , a notation I use in order to save my sanity and forgo me writing “tangent space” everytime). The covariant derivative of along the curve is denoted by

Intuitively, parallel transport moves the vector along the curve while allowing it to change as little as possible. The tangent planes at two different points of a curved surface are different vector spaces, so it does not really make sense to demand that the vector remains literally unchanged. Instead, we demand that it has no change which can be detected within the tangent plane. From the point of view of the surrounding , the ordinary derivative need not vanish, but for a parallel transported vector its tangential projection vanishes and hence any remaining change is purely normal to the surface. In this sense the vector changes only as much as the curvature of the surface forces it to.

Riemann Tensor and Ricci Curvature

With that lengthy discussion of Gauss over with, we can come to the next man of the hour (or two or three depending on how long it takes me to write this): Bernhard Riemann.

We have so far understood curvature by placing a surface inside and watching how its normal vectors change. Riemann’s great leap was to ask how we could recognise curvature if we were trapped entirely within the surface, with no normal direction and no surrounding space available to us. Conveniently, we have already introduced exactly the machinery needed to answer this: covariant derivatives and parallel transport.

Imagine taking a tangent vector at some point and parallel transporting it around a very small closed loop. In a flat plane the vector returns pointing in precisely the same direction. On a curved surface this generally does not happen: when the vector returns to its starting point it will have changed, despite having been parallel transported along every individual part of the loop. The failure of the vector to return unchanged is therefore detecting curvature using only measurements made within the surface.

There is an equivalent infinitesimal way to view the same idea. Let and be two directions and let be the vector we wish to carry around. We can first differentiate in the direction and then in the direction, or perform these operations in the opposite order. If the geometry is flat these two operations agree, whereas on a curved space their difference need not vanish. Curvature is, in this sense, the failure of covariant derivatives to agree. Technically we would say they fail to commute.

We can now make this precise. Let be our surface for the moment, although everything that follows works on a Riemannian manifold of any dimension, and let denote the collection of smooth vector fields on . Given three vector fields , the Riemann curvature operator is defined by

The first two terms are the commutator we have just described. The final term contains the Lie bracket , which measures the failure of the two vector fields themselves to commute. If you haven’t met this object before this is fine, you can think of it in terms of matrices. Marices are said to commute if and only if In the case of vector fields, it is defined by how it acts on any scalar function ,

This correction is necessary because following and then does not always bring us to the same point as following and then . Subtracting removes this discrepancy, leaving only the change due to curvature. In we have what is called a coordinate basis, such that , then the basis vectors commute, so and the final term vanishes. To see this quickly, have these basis vectors act on an arbitrary, differentiable function ,

Since was arbitrary we can say that in general the relation holds for any coordinate basis.

At a first glance appears to depend on derivatives of the vector fields and not merely on the vectors themselves. However, the derivative terms cancel in precisely such a way that, for any smooth scalar function ,

The value of the curvature at a point therefore depends only on the three tangent vectors at that point, rather than on how we extend them to vector fields nearby. is called a Tensor, well more specifically, the Riemann Curvature Tensor. I appreciate that this section is rather long. But, I think it’s worth it to make the physical applications as clear and satisfying as possible. Now, onto the Ricci Tensor and Ricci Curvature.

Ricci Tensor

So I have the Riemann tensor with its 4-indicies. A great man and mathematician (in the trumpiest voice I can do) - Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro - investigated the geometric invariant quantity formed by taking the trace of the Riemann tensor and found the Ricci Tensor. It measures the curvature by understanding how volumes of balls compare to Euclidean space

Using the metric I could write it as

You can derive a coordinate expression for this tensor, similar to that of the Riemann tensor, but I will fight the urge to do so and leave it for you to either google or show yourself. Anyway, what is the geometric intuition behind this object? To think about that I have to discuss Riemann normal coordinates as hinted to just now.

Curvature and Physics

Given the lengthy introduction above to the numerous types of curvature, I will now give a view of why it is useful and necessary in phyiscs. I also want to try and convince you of the theoretical power of geometry in physics.

Geometry and Gravity

You are probably familiar with the idea that gravity is a force. This is the Newtonian picture of gravity, which is very useful for many applications. However, it is not the most fundamental description of gravity. The more fundamental description is given by Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity, which describes gravity as a manifestation of the curvature of spacetime.

The language of this is differential geometry, which we have been developing. The idea is that massive objects cause spacetime to curve, and this curvature affects the motion of objects. In this picture, what we perceive as the force of gravity is actually the result of objects following geodesics in curved spacetime. So, in that sense gravity isn’t really a force at all, but rather a manifestation of the geometry of spacetime. Spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold, with three spatial dimensions and one time dimension. The curvature of spacetime is described by the Riemann curvature tensor, which we have discussed above. The Einstein field equations relate the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of matter and energy, and they are given by

where is the energy-momentum tensor, is the gravitational constant, is the speed of light, and is the cosmological constant. The left-hand side of the equation describes the curvature of spacetime, while the right-hand side describes the distribution of matter and energy. The Einstein field equations are a set of ten interrelated differential equations that describe how matter and energy influence the curvature of spacetime, and they form the foundation of our understanding of gravity in the context of general relativity. As a simple example, consider the case where we have no matter in our universe and no cosmological constant, so that and . In this case, the Einstein field equations reduce to

We can take the trace of this equation by contracting with the inverse metric , which gives

This is a simple example of how the Einstein field equations relate the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of matter and energy. I should be careful here though: Ricci flat does not mean flat. Recall that the Ricci tensor only records the trace of the Riemann tensor (the net focusing of a bundle of geodesics). The remaining trace-free part, called the Weyl tensor, is free to be non-zero even in empty space. This is how tidal forces and gravitational waves can exist where there is no matter at all. Flat Minkowski space is the simplest vacuum solution, but it is far from the only one.

The simplest, non-trivial solution to the Einstein field equations is the Schwarzschild solution, which describes the spacetime geometry outside a spherically symmetric, non-rotating mass. The Schwarzschild metric is given by where is the mass of the object, and are the Schwarzschild coordinates. This is a vacuum solution, so its Ricci tensor vanishes everywhere outside the mass. Its Riemann tensor, however, does not. A convenient check is the Kretschmann scalar,

which is clearly non-zero, so the spacetime is indeed curved (and genuinely singular at ). The Schwarzschild solution has been extensively tested and confirmed through observations, such as the bending of light around massive objects (gravitational lensing) and the precession of planetary orbits.

Geometry and Gauge Theories

The standard model of particle physics is a gauge theory, which describes the fundamental forces of nature (except for gravity) in terms of symmetries and fields. In this framework, the interactions between particles are mediated by gauge bosons, which are associated with the symmetries of the theory. The mathematical structure of gauge theories is deeply connected to differential geometry, as the gauge fields can be interpreted as ``connections on principal bundles’’, and the field strengths correspond to curvature forms. I won’t be super rigorous here, but the idea is that the gauge fields can be thought of as providing a way to compare vectors in different tangent spaces, similar to how the Levi-Civita connection allows us to compare vectors in different tangent spaces on a manifold. In this sense they are themselves connections of the theory. The curvature of the gauge fields then encodes information about the interactions between particles, and the dynamics of the gauge fields are governed by equations that are analogous to the Einstein field equations in general relativity.

Let’s see this in a bit more detail. Consider a gauge theory with a gauge group , which is a Lie group that describes the symmetries of the theory. The gauge fields are represented by a connection , which is a Lie algebra-valued one-form on spacetime. The field strength is then given by the curvature of the connection, which can be expressed as where is the exterior derivative and is the wedge product. The field strength encodes the information about the interactions between particles, and it satisfies the Bianchi identity, which is a generalization of the second Bianchi identity we discussed earlier. The dynamics of the gauge fields are governed by the Yang-Mills equations, which are analogous to the Einstein field equations in general relativity. The Yang-Mills equations can be derived from an action principle, and they describe how the gauge fields evolve in response to the presence of matter and other gauge fields. The curvature of the gauge fields plays a central role in determining the behavior of particles and their interactions, and it is intimately connected to the symmetries of the theory. In this way, differential geometry provides a powerful framework for understanding the fundamental forces of nature and the interactions between particles in the context of gauge theories.

The easiest one we can look at is the gauge theory, which describes electromagnetism. In this case, the gauge group is , and the gauge field corresponds to the electromagnetic potential. The field strength is then given by which is the familiar electromagnetic field tensor given by the matrix The Bianchi identity in this case reduces to the statement which corresponds to the homogeneous Maxwell equations. The dynamics of the electromagnetic field are governed by the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations, which can be derived from the action principle and are given by where is the Hodge star operator and is the current one-form (up to a sign that depends on your conventions).

Geometry and Beyond the Standard Model Physics

So we now have two theories, both built on curvature. General relativity describes gravity through the curvature of the Levi-Civita connection, and the standard model describes the other three forces through the curvature of gauge connections. Between them they describe essentially every experiment we have ever done. However, the standard model is not the end of the story. It says nothing about gravity at the quantum level, it contains nothing that could be dark matter, in its original form it gives neutrinos no mass (they have one), and it has around nineteen free parameters which we simply have to measure and put in by hand. It also offers no explanation for why matter comes in exactly three copies, or generations, of quarks and leptons.

Attempts to fix these problems get lumped together under the name beyond the standard model (BSM) physics. There are far too many proposals to cover here, and most of them are yet to be tested. Instead, I want to convince you that a surprising number of the best ideas are geometric at heart, and that the curvature we spent so long building up above is doing most of the heavy lifting.

This is the deepest reason we need to go beyond the standard model, and it is why so many of the ideas below are really attempts to put gravity and gauge theory on the same geometric footing.

A Grand Unified Theory (GUT) proposes that they are all pieces of a single connection for a bigger group. The original example is , due to Georgi and Glashow in 1974. These predict towers of Kaluza-Klein particles, which have been searched for at the LHC (so far without success).

Holonomy and the Shape of Hidden Dimensions

We have seen that extra dimensions can hide, so long as they are small. String theory goes further and requires them: the superstring is only consistent in ten dimensions, so six of them must be curled up into some compact manifold . The obvious question is which one, and the answer is controlled by an object we have already met in disguise.

Recall that when we parallel transport a vector around a closed loop it generally comes back changed. Let’s fix a point and collect together the parallel transport maps around every loop based at . These maps can be composed (go around one loop then the other) and inverted (go around the loop backwards), so they form a group, called the holonomy group,

Since we showed that parallel transport preserves lengths and angles, every is a rotation (or reflection), so for an -dimensional manifold the holonomy group sits inside . On a flat torus, every vector comes back unchanged and the holonomy is trivial. On a sphere, a vector carried around a loop comes back rotated by an angle equal to over the region the loop encloses (Gauss-Bonnet again!), so the holonomy is the full rotation group . In general, for small loops the holonomy is generated by the Riemann tensor, so holonomy is really the global version of curvature.

For a generic oriented six-dimensional manifold the holonomy group is . The most famous Calabi-Yau, the quintic, has and therefore predicts generations, which is rather too many. The Tian-Yau manifold has , giving exactly three. So one of the great unexplained numbers of the standard model becomes the integral of curvature over a hidden space. I think Gauss would have been quite pleased.

I should temper the excitement a little. There are an enormous number of Calabi-Yau manifolds (hundreds of millions are known from just one construction, and nobody knows whether the list is finite). Their size and shape can also be varied continuously, and each such deformation shows up in four dimensions as a massless scalar field, called a modulus, which we do not observe and so must somehow be given a mass. People have found compactifications with exactly the particle content of the (supersymmetric) standard model, but getting all of the masses and couplings right, and fixing the moduli, is still an open problem. And of course there is not yet any experimental evidence for strings at all. Even so, the fact that the question “how many generations are there?” can be turned into a question about curvature and topology is, to me, one of the most remarkable things in theoretical physics.

Final Thoughts

We started with a circle and asked how quickly its tangent vector turns. From there we went through Euler’s principal curvatures, Gauss’s fundamental forms and his Theorema egregium, and Riemann’s realisation that curvature can be detected from inside a space by parallel transporting a vector around a loop, or equivalently by the failure of covariant derivatives to commute. That single commutator then gave us Einstein’s gravity, the field strengths of the standard model and, beyond it, Kaluza-Klein theory, monopoles, axions and the shape of hidden dimensions.

If there is one lesson to take away, it is the one I hinted at right back in the section on parameterisation invariance. Coordinates, parameters and gauges are all just labels, which we are free to choose however makes our lives easiest. The physics lives in the things that do not care about these choices: curvature, holonomy, and the integers that come from integrating curvature over closed spaces. It is no coincidence that so many attempts to go beyond the standard model start by asking a geometric question.

What we still do not have is a theory in which gravity and gauge theory are truly on the same footing at the quantum level. Their geometry is almost identical, but their dynamics are not, and that gap is where much of the most exciting work in theoretical physics is happening today.

If you made it this far, thank you (and well done). I hope you now see curvature the way I do: as one of the deepest and most useful ideas we have.
